Describe the part played by Southern Rhodesia in the Second World War.

points.description: Declared war alongside Britain in September 1939.
Rhodesian African Rifles raised (1940) and fought in Burma.
White Rhodesians served in many theatres, many as airmen in the RAF.
Rhodesian Air Training Group trained thousands of Allied aircrew; minerals and food supplied.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Southern Rhodesia declared war alongside Britain in September 1939. It raised the Rhodesian African Rifles in 1940, which fought in Burma, and white Rhodesians served in many theatres, especially as RAF airmen. The colony hosted the Rhodesian Air Training Group, which trained thousands of Allied aircrew, and supplied minerals and food.

stem: Explain why Operation Barbarossa failed to defeat the USSR in 1941.

points.description: Identifies the Russian winter / lack of winter equipment.
Explains that the cold halted the German advance before Moscow in December 1941.
Identifies the size of the USSR and long supply lines.
Explains that German forces were stretched thin and supplies could not keep up.
Identifies Soviet resistance and resources (reserves, factories moved east).
Explains that the Red Army kept replacing its losses and counter-attacked at Moscow.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The German army was not equipped for the Russian winter, and the freezing cold halted its advance before Moscow in December 1941. The USSR was so vast that German supply lines became very long, and fuel, food and ammunition could not keep up. The Soviets also resisted fiercely: they moved factories east of the Urals, raised new armies from their huge population and launched a counter-attack at Moscow.

hints: Think about weather, distance and the Soviet response.

stem: Explain **two** ways in which the Second World War encouraged decolonisation in Africa.

points.description: Identifies weakened European powers.
Explains that Britain and France were exhausted and indebted, so less able to hold their empires.
Identifies returning African servicemen / ideas of freedom (Atlantic Charter).
Explains that ex-servicemen had new experiences and expectations, and Allied talk of self-determination was turned against colonial rule.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: First, the war left Britain and France exhausted and in debt, so they were less able to keep control of their empires. Second, African ex-servicemen returned with new experiences and expectations, and nationalists used the Allies' own language of freedom and self-determination, as in the Atlantic Charter, against colonial rule.

hints: Think about the colonial powers and about Africans who served.

stem:
Study the source and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a letter from a fictional African soldier of the Rhodesian African Rifles to his brother, written from a camp in Asia in 1945 (invented for this question)

> We have sailed across the sea and now wait to go to Burma. The officers tell us we fight so that all peoples may be free. I have met Indian soldiers who say the same, and who say that after the war they will rule their own country. My brother, when I come home I will ask why a man who fought for freedom must still carry a pass in his own land.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What does Source A suggest about the experiences of African soldiers in the war?

points.description: They travelled far from home / met soldiers from other colonies such as India.
They were told they were fighting for freedom.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How might experiences like those in Source A have affected African politics after 1945? Use your own knowledge.

points.description: Soldiers questioned colonial restrictions (passes, land, wages).
Contact with Indian nationalism showed that independence was possible (India independent 1947).
Ex-servicemen joined or supported nationalist movements.
Allied promises of freedom (Atlantic Charter) used to demand rights.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How far was the experience of African soldiers the main reason why the Second World War led to decolonisation? Use the source and your own knowledge.

points.description: Soldiers' experience: new ideas and expectations, as in the source.
Other: weakening of Britain and France (debt, exhaustion).
Other: superpowers (USA, USSR) and the UN opposed colonial empires.
Other: Indian independence (1947) as an example; growth of nationalist parties and towns.
Limit: the source is one fictional soldier's view; many ex-servicemen did not become active nationalists.
Supported judgement.

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The experience of African soldiers, as Source A suggests, mattered: men who had travelled to India and Burma and been told they fought for freedom came home less willing to accept pass laws and low wages, and some supported nationalist movements. However, other results of the war were probably more important. Britain and France were exhausted and in debt, the USA and the USSR both opposed old-style empires, and the new United Nations supported self-determination. India's independence in 1947 showed what was possible, and wartime industry and urban growth helped nationalist parties to recruit. Not every ex-serviceman became politically active. Overall soldiers' experience was one important factor, but the weakening of the colonial powers and the new world order did more to make decolonisation possible.

hints: Think about what the writer learned and how he might act after the war.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: "The Eastern Front was the most important reason for the defeat of Germany." How far do you agree?

points.description: Eastern Front: most German forces and losses there; Stalingrad and Kursk destroyed German strength.
Eastern Front: Soviet manpower and industry; Red Army reached Berlin.
Other: USA's industrial power and Lend-Lease supplies (including to the USSR).
Other: D-Day and the second front; strategic bombing; war at sea.
Other: Hitler's mistakes (Barbarossa, declaring war on the USA, refusing retreats).
Supported judgement.

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The Eastern Front was very important. Most of the German army fought there for most of the war, and it suffered most of its losses there. At Stalingrad Germany lost an entire army, and after the Battle of Kursk in 1943 it could no longer launch major offensives. The USSR, with its huge population and factories moved east of the Urals, kept replacing its losses, and the Red Army captured Berlin in 1945.

However, other factors mattered. American industry produced vast quantities of weapons and supplies, some of which, under Lend-Lease, kept the Soviet army moving. D-Day opened a second front in June 1944, and Allied bombing and the war at sea weakened German production. Hitler also made serious mistakes: invading the USSR before defeating Britain, declaring war on the USA, and forbidding retreats.

Overall I largely agree: the Eastern Front destroyed the bulk of the German army, but Soviet victory depended partly on American supplies and on the pressure of the Western Allies, so it was the most important but not the only reason.

parts.explanation: Both sides and a supported judgement.

hints: In (b), compare the Eastern Front with the other theatres.
